kinds.gravel_pit: gravel pit in old river gravel
kinds.terrace_cut: road cut through old river gravel
kinds.terrace_edge: terrace edge: a riser or gully face

dig.gravel_pit: Work the pit walls and the spoil heaps: the whole thickness of the old bar is open, with the top lag at the rim and the heavy stones at the floor.
dig.terrace_cut: Walk the cut face: the lag sits in the first foot under the soil line, the heavy stones at the base of the gravel.
dig.terrace_edge: Dig into the face where a gully or the riser has already opened it; rain re-sorts the slope below it every winter.
dig.old_bar: Scrape the first foot: the lag of tough stones sits right under the sod. Look first at rodent burrows, fence lines and any bare patch.

rules.land: every status, with its 100 m grade; the app hides what the land filter excludes
rules.text: Stranded river gravel: terraces, outwash, Ice Age flood bars and fans the map names, 2-120 m above the river that built them, within 150 m of a road a car can use, where a gravel pit, a road cut, a riser or gully, or the flat terrace top opens the old bar up. A bar the river left keeps every stone it had, and rain and wind strip the fines so the toughest stones sit as a lag right under the soil. Ranked by the chance that a target stone is really in the gravel: reported finds within 3 km, finds upstream on the river that built it, and the map unit's own words (agate, petrified wood, quartzite) carry the weight; the stone map only nudges. What the old river carried comes from the source rock it cut upstream, the same bedrock then as now, with a flood prior for the Missoula flood bars. Not yet tested against trips.

spots.label: terrace edge: a riser or gully face
spots.builder_why: the river that built this terrace still runs below it, so what it cut upstream then is what it cuts now
spots.under_text: gravel at the surface (bare ground in the satellite view)
spots.dig: Dig into the face where a gully or the riser has already opened it; rain re-sorts the slope below it every winter.
expect: Most of the gravel: pale rhyolite and tuff and dark basalt cobbles (keep the ones with white-filled gas pockets).
Zeolites: white radiating crystals in the gas pockets of basalt cobbles.
Agate & jasper: waxy, translucent or banded chalcedony pebbles; backlight anything that glows.
Geodes & thundereggs: knobbly round nodules that feel heavy and ring when tapped.
Opal: glassy or milky seams and bubbles in basalt chunks, soft enough for a knife to scratch.
Terrace stones wear a dull weathered rind and sometimes a white caliche crust: wet them or crack one before you judge.
spots.why: A terrace edge: a riser or gully face above John Day River, 6 m above the river, 110 ft from S Twickenham Rd. Odds of a target stone: good (96%): zeolites 91%, agate & jasper 31%, geodes & thundereggs 15%, opal 14%. Zeolites: 2 reported within 3 km; 25 upstream on the river that built it. What the old river carried: agate & jasper, zeolites, geodes & thundereggs, opal (agate & jasper ground cut right there). Confidence: same river, the river that built this terrace still runs below it, so what it cut upstream then is what it cuts now.

spots.under_text: gravel at the surface (bare ground in the satellite view)
spots.dig: Work the pit walls and the spoil heaps: the whole thickness of the old bar is open, with the top lag at the rim and the heavy stones at the floor.
expect: Most of the gravel: dark basalt cobbles (keep the ones with white-filled gas pockets).
Opal: glassy or milky seams and bubbles in basalt chunks, soft enough for a knife to scratch.
Agate & jasper: waxy, translucent or banded chalcedony pebbles; backlight anything that glows.
Garnet: dark red grains in the black sand at bar heads; a gold pan finds them.
Quartz crystals: milky or clear quartz chunks, sometimes with flat crystal faces.
Terrace stones wear a dull weathered rind and sometimes a white caliche crust: wet them or crack one before you judge.
spots.why: A gravel pit in old river gravel above Potholes Canal, 6 m above the river, 200 ft from K 5. Odds of a target stone: good (99%): opal 83%, agate & jasper 66%, garnet 52%, quartz crystals 37%. Opal: 2 reported within 3 km; 1 upstream on the river that built it. What the old river carried: agate & jasper, quartz crystals, zeolites, petrified wood (agate & jasper ground cut upstream). Confidence: Ice Age flood bar, left by the Missoula floods: the whole Clark Fork basin plus everything scoured on the way; the proven Columbia bars are this kind.

Zeolites: white radiating crystals in the gas pockets of basalt cobbles.
Staurolite & kyanite: brown crosses or blue blades in pebbles of schist.
Opal: glassy or milky seams and bubbles in basalt chunks, soft enough for a knife to scratch.
Garnet: dark red grains in the black sand at bar heads; a gold pan finds them.
Terrace stones wear a dull weathered rind and sometimes a white caliche crust: wet them or crack one before you judge.
spots.why: A old bar: flat terrace top above Hangman Creek, 66 m above the river, 400 ft from S Baltimore Rd. Odds of a target stone: good (89%): zeolites 58%, staurolite & kyanite 53%, opal 14%, garnet 12%. Zeolites: 1 reported within 3 km. What the old river carried: zeolites, opal, agate & jasper, garnet (zeolites ground cut right there). Confidence: Ice Age flood bar, left by the Missoula floods: the whole Clark Fork basin plus everything scoured on the way; the proven Columbia bars are this kind.
